pages.summary: Columns of data of any class (variables), one row per observation, each variable with a name.
body: A table holds variables of the same height side by side: numbers, text, datetimes, categoricals, even matrices or other tables. Variables are named after the variables given (else `Var1`, `Var2`, ...). `T.Name` is a variable; `T(rows, vars)` is a smaller table and `T{rows, vars}` the data put together, where rows and vars are numbers, masks, `:` or names. `T.Name = x` adds a variable, `T(rows, :) = []` deletes rows, `T(end+1, :) = {v1, ..., vN}` adds one, and `[T1; T2]` and `[T1, T2]` put tables together. `T.Properties` holds the variable names, row names, units, descriptions and the table's description, each set by assignment.
syntax: Of a size, its variables of these types.

examples.title: A table made, read and grown
examples.output:
T = 

  3×3 table

     Name      Born      Field
    _______    ____    _________

    "Ada"      1815    maths
    "Alan"     1912    maths
    "Grace"    1906    computing

ans =

        1815        1912        1906

ans = 

  2×3 table

     Name      Born      Field
    _______    ____    _________

    "Alan"     1912    maths
    "Grace"    1906    computing

ans =

   114

T = 

  4×4 table

      Name      Born      Field      Age
    ________    ____    _________    ___

    "Ada"       1815    maths        211
    "Alan"      1912    maths        114
    "Grace"     1906    computing    120
    "Edsger"    1930    computing     96

body: `istable` is true for a table, `istimetable` for a timetable, `istabular` for either.

examples.title: A table, a timetable, a matrix

pages.summary: A table's numbers of rows and variables; its first and last rows.
body: `height` is the number of rows (of an array, `size(A, 1)`), `width` the number of variables (of an array, `size(A, 2)`); a variable of several columns counts once. `head` and `tail` give the first or last k rows (8 unless given), to look at a long table.

examples.title: A long table looked at
examples.code:
T = table((1:100)', sqrt((1:100)'), 'VariableNames', {'n', 'root'});
[height(T) width(T)]
head(T, 3)
tail(T, 2)

pages.summary: Picks a table's variables of a type.
body: Used as the variable index, `T(:, vartype(type))` keeps the variables of that type: `'numeric'` (numbers of any class), `'cellstr'`, or a class name such as `'logical'`, `'string'`, `'datetime'` or `'categorical'`.

ans =

    x    k
    _    _

ans =

     ok
    _____

    true

pages.summary: Tables made from arrays, cells and structs, and turned back into them.
body: `table2array` puts the variables together as one array (they must go together: numbers with numbers, text with text); `table2cell` gives a cell for each row and variable; `table2struct` a struct for each row, or one struct of variables (`'ToScalar'`). `array2table` makes each column of a matrix a variable, `cell2table` each column of a cell array (numbers becoming numeric variables), and `struct2table` each field of a struct array.
syntax: A struct array, one element per row.

examples.title: There and back
examples.output:
T = 

  3×2 table

    x    y
    _    _

    1    2
    3    4
    5    6

ans =

     1     3     5
     2     4     6

ans = 

  struct with fields:

    x: 3
    y: 4

U = 

  2×2 table

      Part       Mass
    _________    ____

    {'pump' }    4.5
    {'valve'}    0.8

ans = 

  2×2 cell array

    {'pump'}     {[4.5000]}
    {'valve'}    {[0.8000]}

ans = 

  2×2 table

    a      b
    _    _____

    1    {'p'}
    2    {'q'}

pages.summary: Variables added, removed, moved and renamed.
body: Each gives a new table. `addvars` adds variables at the end, or before or after one (named after the inputs, or `'NewVariableNames'`); `removevars` removes them; `movevars` moves them before or after one (to the end with neither); `renamevars` renames them. Variables are named, given by position, or picked by a mask or `vartype`.

examples.title: Rearranging a table
examples.output:
T = 

  2×3 table

    id    a    b
    __    _    _

    10    1    3
    20    2    4

T = 

  2×2 table

    second    first
    ______    _____

      3         1
      4         2

pages.summary: Variables split and merged, a table turned, and variables converted.
body: `splitvars` makes each variable of several columns (or a table inside a table) one variable per column, named after it; `mergevars` puts variables together as one, where the first stood; `rows2vars` turns the table so that its rows become variables (the old names in `OriginalVariableNames`); `convertvars` converts variables to a type (`'double'`, `'string'`, `'categorical'`, `'datetime'` and the like) or through a function.

examples.title: Turned, and text made categorical
examples.output:
ans =

    OriginalVariableNames    r1    r2
    _____________________    __    __

            {'a'}            1     2
            {'b'}            3     4

ans =
